APPLICATION PAPER

Foreword | Why I wrote this

Data governance has to leave the conference room and enter the work.

For 30 years, I have worked where public responsibility meets the physical reality of water. I have seen the work from the regulatory side and from the operator's chair. From both seats, the same truth keeps returning: a utility can own excellent systems and still struggle to explain which answer is authoritative, who accepted it and what evidence stands behind the decision.

That is why I wrote this paper. I did not want to add another abstract definition of data governance. I wanted to make the work operational. If we use the word One in One Water, we should be able to show what One means across control systems, assets, laboratories, models, customers, regulation and the decisions that connect them. If we say artificial intelligence (AI) governance or data governance, we should be able to name the person, the control, the evidence and the outcome.

The point

A transaction closes a task. A transformation changes the way a utility decides, operates and learns. Our work should create transformational systems, not a larger collection of disconnected transactions.


AI will change utility work. The harder question is whether utilities will prepare their data before placing more decisions on top of it. If the data cannot be found, joined, understood, traced and challenged, AI will not create transformation. It will automate uncertainty and make weak decisions move faster.

In critical infrastructure, this is not a minor technology problem. Data shapes service, safety, compliance, capital, customer and emergency decisions. When a serious incident occurs, people will ask what information was used, where it came from, who approved it and what warning was missed. The utility should be able to answer before the incident, not after it.

This paper joins the world of standards, provenance, controls, quality, privacy, cybersecurity and AI to the physical and public work of a utility. A standard becomes useful when it changes a handoff, a decision, a control or a result. Your data is part of your utility. Govern it with the same seriousness as the assets, money and public trust that depend on it.

APPLICATION PAPER

Executive summary

Utilities do not need another governance slogan. They need an operating system for accountable data decisions.

The central finding is direct: a utility becomes AI-ready by becoming data-ready first. The work is not a technology cleanup exercise. It is the operating discipline that makes consequential decisions explainable, testable and improvable.

Three conclusions

  1. No single standard completes the job. The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) supplies governance direction. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) supplies portable provenance and data descriptions. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) supply control, risk and assurance methods. Law, regulation and utility context determine what must operate.

  2. The utility is one decision system. Control, operational history, mapping, modeling, maintenance, laboratory, meter, customer, finance, regulatory and AI data must connect through shared identity, meaning, ownership, lineage, quality and rights.

  3. A score without evidence is an opinion. Maturity, evidence confidence, consequence and urgency must remain visible. Progress is demonstrated by recurring operation, measured results, verified closure and better decisions over time.

What a utility should be able to prove

  • Which source was authoritative for the material decision and why it was fit for that use.

  • How identity, time, units, location, version and quality survived each system handoff.

  • Who owned the data, who could change it and who accepted any exception or residual risk.

  • How the answer moved from physical source through transformation, model or spreadsheet to action and outcome.

  • What a regulator, auditor, operator, customer or incident team can review later.

Executive decision

Treat data readiness as utility readiness. Fund it as an operating capability tied to service, safety, resilience, affordability, compliance and capital delivery. Do not leave it as a technology cleanup project.


The application in one sentence

Build a governed evidence chain from the physical source to the public outcome, use it to locate the current maturity and twin phase, then improve the highest-consequence decisions first.

APPLICATION PAPER

1. Why utility data governance matters now

The issue is not whether a utility has data. The issue is whether it can use the data with accountability.

Most utilities already own the source systems. They have supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA), operational historians, a geographic information system (GIS), advanced metering infrastructure (AMI), customer and billing platforms, a computerized maintenance management system (CMMS) or enterprise asset management (EAM) platform, a laboratory information management system (LIMS), finance tools and many local spreadsheets. The weakness sits above and between them. The organization often cannot answer, quickly and consistently, what data exists, what it means, how it connects, who owns it and whether it is safe to use for a specific decision.

More data is not better data

The volume of data created, captured, copied and consumed globally was estimated at 64.2 zettabytes in 2020, while a pre-2025 European Commission forecast placed 2025 at 175 zettabytes, nearly three times as much in five years. One zettabyte equals 1,000 exabytes, 1 million petabytes or 1 billion terabytes; the correct term is petabyte, not penderbyte. Yet quantity is not quality: without identity, context, ownership, lineage, controls and fitness for purpose, more data creates more noise, duplication and risk rather than better decisions. [DG01] [DG02]


Figure 1. The missing layer above utility systems

What this shows. Utilities usually have the source systems. The gap is the governed layer that identifies data, states what it means, names who is accountable, records how it changed, and tells a user whether it is fit for a decision.

Source: APAS AI synthesis based on the standards and utility research in this paper.

Governance is the way a decision becomes accountable

A policy is part of governance, but it is not the whole of governance. Governance is visible when a utility can point to a decision right, a named owner, an operating control, a retained record and a way to correct failure. If any one of those parts is missing, the utility has a statement of intent, not a dependable capability.

A practical test

Can a qualified new team member find, access, join and understand the data needed for a material decision without relying on one person who knows where everything is hidden? If the answer is no, the organization has knowledge risk and data risk at the same time.


The utility consequences

Decision area

What weak governance looks like

What good governance changes

Operations

Alarm, sensor or network data is used without time, unit, calibration or source context.

The operator sees source, quality state, freshness, exception and the approved rule.

Assets and capital

GIS, drawings, EAM and field records disagree about the same asset.

A governed identifier and version process connects the physical asset to the work and decision.

Customer

Interval use, estimates, corrections and eligibility decisions cannot be reconstructed.

Purpose, source, estimation, approval, notice and correction evidence travel with the output.

Regulatory

A reported number is rebuilt through spreadsheets and personal knowledge.

The filing traces to authoritative data, transformations, reconciliations and sign-off.

AI and analytics

A model is deployed before the data is shown to be suitable and representative.

The use case has named accountability, data provenance, tests, limits, monitoring and retirement rules.


The risk of moving faster on weak foundations

AI can reduce effort, improve pattern detection and help people ask better questions. It can also create a faster mess. When a model draws from data that is late, incomplete, misjoined, mislabeled or outside its approved purpose, the error can travel farther than the original record ever could.

A utility should expect questions after any material failure: Which version was used? Which source was authoritative? Was the data fit for this use? Who approved the exception? What changed? Was the result challenged? The governance program should be designed to answer those questions as part of normal work.

2. The terms that matter

Clear terms prevent weak controls from hiding behind broad language.

Figure 2. Lineage, provenance and integrity answer different questions

What this shows. Lineage shows the route. Provenance explains the history and responsibility. Integrity provides evidence that the data and its history were not altered outside the approved process.

Source: APAS AI synthesis of the W3C Provenance Data Model (PROV) and NIST control concepts.

Plain-language definitions

Term

Plain meaning

Utility example

Evidence to retain

Data governance

The decisions, responsibilities, controls and proof used to direct data work.

The utility decides which network model is authoritative and who can approve a change.

Charter, decision, owner, control result and review.

Data management

The work that creates, stores, protects, moves, improves and disposes of data.

A data team validates AMI files, resolves exceptions and publishes a governed product.

Run record, rule result, issue, version and service level.

Lineage

The route from source through transformation to use.

A regulatory leakage value traces to sensors, work records, mappings and calculations.

Source, job, input, output, version, time and consumer.

Provenance

The fuller history of the data, the activity and the responsible actor.

A laboratory result records sample, method, instrument, analyst, approval and amendment.

Entity, activity, agent, purpose, time, version and relationship.

Integrity

Confidence that data and evidence remain complete and protected from improper change.

A control detects an unauthorized change to an approved reporting dataset.

Authorization, validation, audit log, hash or signature, recovery test.

Data quality

Fitness for a stated use, not a claim that data is perfect.

Fifteen-minute meter data may fit a customer trend but not a second-by-second control decision.

Use, rule, threshold, result, exception and accepted limit.

Traceability

The ability to follow a requirement, record or decision backward and forward.

A customer complaint connects to the bill, estimate, meter event, correction and notice.

Linked identifiers and dated records across the chain.

Data product

A governed dataset, application programming interface (API) or feature set with an owner and service promise.

A network-risk feature set used by capital planning and field operations.

Contract, owner, schema, quality, lineage, rights and lifecycle.


The minimum provenance event

A useful provenance record does not need to be complicated. For a critical transformation, retain the input identifiers, output identifier, activity or run identifier, responsible person or service, time, code or configuration version, quality result, purpose, approval and integrity evidence. The W3C Provenance Data Model (PROV) provides the entity, activity and agent pattern for this work. OpenLineage provides a practical job, run and dataset pattern. [W01] [W02] [U06]

A utility-specific rule for quality

Fitness comes before score

Do not ask whether a dataset is good. Ask whether it is fit for this decision, at this time, with this consequence. Record the answer and the accepted limits.


Quality is contextual. A location that is adequate for customer communication may be unsafe for excavation. A meter interval that is adequate for billing analysis may not be adequate for operational control. A governance program should tie each quality requirement to the use, criticality and consequence. [I05] [I06] [I10] [W04]

APPLICATION PAPER

3. How the standards fit together

Use the standards as one control system. Do not force one source to answer every question.

Figure 3. No single standard does the whole job

What this shows. Law and policy set obligations. ISO sets governance and management direction. W3C provides machine-readable evidence models. NIST and IEC provide control and assurance methods. Industry frameworks help organize capability.

Source: APAS AI standards crosswalk.

ISO gives the governing and management structure

ISO/IEC 38505-1 sets principles for the governance of data. The ISO/IEC 5259 series brings data quality into analytics and machine learning (ML), including measures, management, process and governance. ISO/IEC 11179 supports metadata registries and dataset registration. ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO/IEC 23894 address AI management and risk. ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701 and ISO 15489 connect security, privacy, personally identifiable information (PII) and records. ISO 55001 and ISO 24516 connect the data work to assets and water utility performance. [I01] [I04-I08] [I14] [I16-I18] [I20-I26]

W3C makes the evidence portable

W3C PROV models provenance through entities, activities and agents. The Data Catalog Vocabulary (DCAT) describes catalogs and datasets. The Data Quality Vocabulary (DQV) expresses quality. The Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL) tests graph constraints. The Open Digital Rights Language (ODRL) expresses rights and duties. Verifiable Credentials Data Integrity adds cryptographic proof patterns. The Resource Description Framework (RDF), Simple Knowledge Organization System (SKOS) and JavaScript Object Notation for Linked Data (JSON-LD) support identifiers, relationships and shared meaning. These are technical building blocks for evidence that can move between systems. [W01-W11]

NIST organizes risk, controls and assurance

NIST does not publish one formal standard called data governance. Its contribution is spread across the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), the Research Data Framework, the provenance glossary, Special Publication (SP) 800-53 controls, SP 800-53A assessment procedures, the Cybersecurity Framework, the Privacy Framework, supply-chain guidance and the Open Security Controls Assessment Language (OSCAL). Together, these sources help a utility define risk, select controls, test them and exchange assurance information. [N01-N10]

Figure 4. Standards translated into utility jobs

What this shows. The useful question is not which standard wins. The useful question is which operating job each source helps a utility perform and what evidence should remain after the job is done.

Source: APAS AI standards crosswalk.

APPLICATION PAPER

4. The utility operating model

Govern the physical decision chain, not only the information technology estate.

Information technology (IT) manages business and information services. OT monitors or controls the physical process. Utility governance must connect both because a material decision often begins in physical equipment and ends in a business, customer or regulatory record.

Figure 5. The governed data lifecycle

What this shows. Governance must stay with the data from creation through use and disposal. Every handoff needs identity, responsibility, quality, change, access, purpose and retention evidence.

Source: APAS AI synthesis of ISO, W3C, NIST and records-management sources.

The lifecycle evidence rule

At each lifecycle stage, the utility should retain enough evidence to answer seven questions: What is it? Who is accountable? What changed? Is it fit for this use? Who can access it? Why is it being used? How long should it remain? The answers do not have to live in one tool, but they must connect through stable identifiers.

Figure 6. The utility data estate is one connected system

What this shows. Operational, asset, laboratory, customer, work, regulatory and AI data depend on common identifiers and controlled handoffs. Governing only the enterprise warehouse leaves the most consequential utility decisions outside the program.

Source: APAS AI utility operating model.

The connective tissue is shared identity

The systems do not need to become one platform. They do need to agree on the identity of the asset, event, obligation and decision. Stable identifiers allow a person to move from a physical condition to the supporting record without rebuilding the story by hand.

  • An asset identifier connects the geographic information system, maintenance record, telemetry tag and engineering model to the same physical thing.

  • Event identifiers and trusted time connect an alarm, sample, customer impact, work response and operating outcome.

  • Rule and obligation identifiers connect a permit limit or operating rule to the calculation, approval, filing and corrective action it governs.

Figure 14. One utility question crosses the entire data estate

What this shows. An overflow-risk, water-quality, compliance or capital question rarely belongs to one system. It depends on controlled connections among SCADA, the historian, GIS, hydraulic models, CMMS or EAM, LIMS, customer systems, weather and regulatory records.

Source: APAS AI utility decision-chain model.

Four examples of fragmented data becoming an accountable outcome

Utility decision

Systems that must connect

Governed outcome

Wet-weather overflow response

SCADA levels and alarms; historian time series; rainfall; GIS collection model; CMMS pump condition and work; fats, oils and grease (FOG) inspections; permit and consent requirements.

A cited risk signal, operator decision, response record and regulatory evidence chain.

Drinking-water quality release

LIMS sample and method; instrument calibration and maintenance; SCADA treatment conditions; historian trends; laboratory approval; distribution model; regulatory limits.

A defensible release or escalation decision with custody, method, condition, approval and exception evidence.

Capital renewal priority

GIS asset identity; CMMS or EAM failure and work history; hydraulic or process model; AMI demand; customer impact; climate stress; cost and regulatory commitments.

A ranked investment decision that can be traced from physical condition and modeled consequence to funding.

Customer leak or billing correction

AMI interval data; meter events; customer information system (CIS) account and billing; GIS service location; field work order; estimation rule; notice and correction history.

A fair, reconstructable customer outcome with purpose, source, estimate, review and redress.


The fragmentation tax

When these systems do not share identifiers, time, meaning and evidence, staff rebuild the truth by hand. The delay is expensive; the inconsistency is a governance risk; and the resulting AI learns the fragmentation rather than resolving it.

Figure 7. A decision is only as strong as its evidence chain

What this shows. A utility should be able to trace a material decision back through the report or model, each transformation, the authoritative source, the accountable people and the control results.

Source: APAS AI evidence-chain method.

Use a material decision as the unit of proof

The fastest way to test governance is to follow one consequential output. Select a regulatory filing, an operational alert, a customer outcome, a capital recommendation or an AI-supported decision. Trace it backward through every transformation to the authoritative source. Then trace it forward to the action, outcome, issue and correction.

The handoff rule

A handoff is governed when the next person or system receives the data, its meaning, its quality state, its approved purpose and the evidence needed to challenge it.

Maturity and evidence are separate

Figure 10. Maturity must be supported by proof

What this shows. A policy can establish intent, but it cannot prove operation. Scores rise only when the utility can show repeatable practice, measured results and independent assurance.

Source: APAS AI maturity and evidence-confidence model.

Level

Name

Meaning

Minimum proof

0

Uncontrolled

The practice is absent, unknown or unreliable.

No dependable proof.

1

Aware

People recognize the need, but work is local or reactive.

Examples or statements, not a controlled method.

2

Defined

A policy, role or method is approved.

Current document, owner and planned process.

3

Operating

The practice is repeated in scope and exceptions are managed.

Operating samples over time.

4

Measured

Performance, coverage and control results are managed.

Metrics, trends, thresholds and corrective action.

5

Assured

Independent testing and learning sustain the practice.

Independent evidence, verified closure and adaptation.


From data chaos to data wisdom and the twin path

Data does not become wisdom simply because it is collected, integrated or analyzed. The value journey begins in data chaos, where records are fragmented and their meaning is uncertain, then moves through governed data, information, knowledge and decision intelligence. Data wisdom is the accountable use of that evidence, combined with operational context, human judgment, consequences and learning; it is an organizational capability, not a database state.

Figure 15. From data chaos to data wisdom and Decision Twin™

What this shows. The value journey turns fragmented records into governed data, usable information, contextual knowledge, decision intelligence and accountable data wisdom. The capability journey begins with discovery and governed connection, supports dependable digital twins, and reaches Decision Twin™ only when rules, evidence, human authority and outcome learning operate together.

Source: APAS AI data-value and maturity model. Decision Twin™ is an APAS trademark.

Phase

What the data can prove

Decision value

0. Discover

Material decisions, source systems, owners and critical gaps are known.

The utility knows where uncertainty and dependency live.

1. Connect

Stable identifiers and controlled interfaces connect selected systems and records.

People can find the same asset, event, customer, sample or rule across systems.

2. Govern

Meaning, quality, ownership, lineage, rights, retention and exceptions operate.

The utility can explain why data is fit for a stated decision.

3. Operational Twin

Current physical state is joined to asset, work, environmental and operator context.

Teams see the operating condition and act with shared context.

4. Digital Twin

The representation can reproduce behavior, test scenarios and compare observed with expected state.

Engineers and operators can simulate consequences before acting.

5. Decision Twin™

The twin connects the model to rules, evidence, accountable authority, alternatives, action and outcome learning.

The utility can explain not only what may happen, but why a decision is permitted, supported and improvable.


Trademark note

Decision Twin™ is an APAS trademark. The term describes a governed decision model that connects operational state, analytical models, rules, evidence, human authority and outcome learning.


Figure 11. The score separates practice from evidence

What this shows. The method records maturity, confidence in the evidence, consequence and urgency separately. That makes the result useful for management instead of turning it into one unexplained number.

Source: APAS AI assessment scoring method.

The scoring method

A key performance indicator (KPI) shows whether a service, control or product is producing the intended result. The assessment keeps those outcome measures separate from the maturity score so activity is not mistaken for value.

Measure

Scale

Rule

Maturity

0 to 5

Record the level of repeatable operating practice.

Evidence confidence

0 to 4

0 absent, 1 asserted, 2 documented, 3 operating sample, 4 independently verified.

Adjusted score

0 to 5

Maturity multiplied by evidence confidence divided by 4. Exclude not-applicable criteria.

Consequence

1 to 5

Rate service, safety, customer, regulatory, financial and trust impact.

Urgency

1 to 5

Rate deadline, incident, audit, project and dependency pressure.

Priority

Relative

Combine the target gap, consequence, exposure and urgency. Keep the factors visible.


Score protection

A criterion cannot score above Level 2 without recurring operating evidence. Independent assurance raises confidence in the proof. It does not raise maturity when the underlying practice is weak.


Assessment evidence starter set

  • Governance charter, policy hierarchy, delegations and recent decisions.

  • System, data and interface inventory with ownership, criticality and jurisdiction.

  • Architecture and flows for SCADA, AMI, GIS, EAM, LIMS, customer, cloud and AI.

  • Lineage and provenance for sampled reports, decisions, customer outputs and AI use cases.

  • Quality rules, results, exceptions, reconciliations, issues and root-cause records.

  • Access, change and audit logs, recovery tests, incidents and supplier assurance.

  • Privacy, AI and transfer assessments, use-case inventories, retention and sharing agreements.

  • Performance reports, internal audit, certification scope, regulatory findings and closure evidence.

Minimum decision samples

Sample

Why it matters

Operational safety or reliability decision

Tests OT identity, time, quality, configuration and operator context.

Regulatory or board report

Tests authoritative source, transformation, reconciliation and sign-off.

Customer bill, alert or eligibility output

Tests personal data, estimates, correction, notice and redress.

Open or shared data product

Tests benefit-risk classification, rights, quality statement and consumer terms.

AI or analytics use case

Tests source rights, suitability, representativeness, evaluation, limits and monitoring.

Supplier or cloud data flow

Tests contract, location, access, assurance, lineage and exit.

APPLICATION PAPER

6. From finding to funded roadmap

An assessment is useful only when it changes ownership, sequence and delivery.

The consulting method

  1. Frame the decisions. Confirm service outcomes, material risks, regulatory commitments, projects and AI use cases that make the work necessary.

  2. Map the estate. Identify systems, interfaces, physical assets, critical data, owners, suppliers, jurisdictions and current programs.

  3. Test the evidence. Review documents, interview by seat and trace selected decisions from source to outcome.

  4. Score and challenge. Record maturity, evidence confidence, consequence, urgency, legal applicability and competing views.

  5. Design the target. Set decision rights, standards, products, controls, platforms, roles, metrics and assurance.

  6. Build the roadmap. Name an owner, action, dependency, cost range, decision date and closure evidence for every material gap.

  7. Implement and verify. Put controls into the work, measure adoption, retest failures and report residual risk.

The roadmap must distinguish transaction from transformation

Transactional output

Transformational outcome

A catalog tool is purchased.

Critical data is owned, described, connected to decisions and kept current.

A governance policy is approved.

People know their decision rights and use them at real handoffs.

A lineage diagram is produced.

Critical pipelines emit usable lineage and support impact analysis and incident review.

A quality dashboard is launched.

Quality requirements are tied to use, owners correct causes and consumers see limits.

An AI review form is added.

Use cases have data provenance, suitability tests, human accountability, monitoring and stop rules.

An audit finding is closed.

The cause is corrected, recurrence is tested and the operating evidence remains available.


The first roadmap horizons

Horizon

Management question

Typical work

0 to 90 days

Where is the immediate decision and evidence risk?

Name owners, select critical decisions, inventory AI uses, control high-risk spreadsheets and trace three to five evidence chains.

3 to 12 months

What operating capability must become repeatable?

Metadata profile, identifiers, data products, stewardship, quality rules, lineage capture, supplier clauses and assurance plan.

12 to 24 months

What should become integrated and measured?

Cross-domain model, automated signals, product portfolio, adoption metrics, regulatory packs and continuous control testing.

24 months and beyond

What can the utility safely scale?

Trusted AI, digital twins, sector data sharing, automated evidence and adaptive governance.


Roadmap rule

Do not create one large data governance project. Build a governed pattern around a material decision, prove the value, then repeat the pattern across the utility.

State and city laws

State and city requirements can add automated-decision, privacy, cyber, records, open-data and employment duties. The assessment should use a jurisdiction register that records covered organization, covered system, covered data or person, geography, trigger, effective date, enforcement authority, evidence owner and next review. Examples in the research set include Colorado, California, New York State, New York City and Texas. [US12-US16]

Legal gate

Before converting a law into a scored criterion, confirm the current text, amendments, definitions, exemptions, commencement, enforcement and whether the public or private utility is covered. Record the interpretation and reviewer. This paper is a research and operating framework, not legal advice.


The applicability record

Field

Question

Organization

Which owner, operator, public body, contractor or supplier is covered?

Service and system

Which critical function, utility service, AI system or automated decision is in scope?

Data and person

Which personal, operational, critical, public, connected-product or training data is covered?

Location

Where are people, assets, processing, storage and recipients located?

Trigger

What action, threshold, risk tier, incident, sharing event or date creates the duty?

Evidence

What proof is retained, who reviews it and when must it be refreshed?

APPLICATION PAPER

8. Reference cases

Use public cases to find patterns. Use internal evidence to score maturity.

Figure 13. Public evidence from three reference cases

What this shows. Anglian Water, Singapore PUB and NEOM show useful signals in open data, smart metering, shared infrastructure and data sovereignty. Public claims are leads for assessment, not proof of enterprise maturity.

Source: Primary public sources from the issuing organizations. See source register C01-C09.

Anglian Water

Anglian Water provides useful public evidence of an open-data program, a release schedule and FAIROE principles: findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable, open and ethical. Its CReDo work shows cross-sector infrastructure data for climate resilience. The Strategic Pipeline Alliance case shows GIS in a common data environment for a digital twin. The utility also reported 1.5 million smart meters in July 2026. [C01-C04]

Pattern

Assessment question

Planned data release

Is there an owned release plan, consumer feedback and a maintained quality statement?

FAIROE and publication risk

Are provenance, quality, ethics, security and misuse risk reviewed before release?

Cross-sector digital twin

Do identifiers, versions, rights and scenario assumptions work across owners?

Smart-meter scale

Are interval quality, privacy, estimation, correction, access and retention controlled?


Singapore PUB

PUB's Smart Water Meter Programme provides a public pattern for secure meter transmission, customer access to usage information and a large coordinated rollout with SP Services. The transferable question is not whether a utility has smart meters. It is whether the utility can govern meter identity, time, estimate, correction, customer access, privacy, security and downstream use at scale. [C05-C06]

NEOM

NEOM and TONOMUS provide public signals around consent-based data, digital infrastructure, private cloud, local requirements and privacy. The case is useful for data sovereignty, platform and new-city design questions. The public sources do not prove enterprise control effectiveness. An assessment should request internal data flows, decision rights, access evidence, retention, supplier terms, incident records and independent assurance. [C07-C09]

Case rule

A press release, website or partner story can identify a practice worth testing. It cannot establish that the practice operates across the enterprise or that its controls are effective.

Turn the paper into a progressive utility product that invites action and supports implementation.

The natural next product

The paper should become the public reasoning layer for a progressive APAS assessment application. A utility enters through a clear scan. The scan explains the risk without pretending to be an audit. It can then invite a consultation, produce an evidence request, create a roadmap and remain connected to the work as controls are implemented.

What the assessment application can look like

The application should make the work visible without reducing it to a single maturity number. The first view tells an executive where the organization stands, which twin phase is supported by evidence and which decision chains need attention first.



Figure 16. Assessment application concept: executive scorecard

What this shows. The executive view shows maturity, evidence confidence, the current twin phase, priority domains and the three decision chains that need attention first. The score is a starting point for action, not an assurance opinion.

Source: APAS AI product concept.

The workbench then opens every score. The assessor can see the question, sampled decision, systems in scope, required evidence, applicable authorities, finding, owner, target and closure proof.

Figure 17. Assessment application concept: evidence workbench

What this shows. Each criterion connects the plain-language question to required evidence, applicable standards, sampled systems, findings, accountable owners and closure proof.

Source: APAS AI product concept.

The final view turns the assessment into continuous improvement. Baseline, target, implementation, retest and verified closure remain connected, so a utility can show progress without pretending that the work is ever permanently finished.

Figure 18. Assessment application concept: continuous improvement

What this shows. The application keeps the assessment alive by showing baseline, target, control implementation, retesting, verified closure and the next review cycle.

Source: APAS AI product concept.

Product guardrails

  • The public scan must state that it is a screening result, not legal advice, certification or an audit opinion.

  • A high score must require evidence. Self-assertion alone cannot produce an assured rating.

  • The application should separate legal applicability, maturity, evidence confidence, consequence and urgency.

  • Connections to utility systems should begin read-only. Each connector needs purpose, scope, permission, logging and an exit path.

  • Sensitive operational, customer and security data should be minimized. The product should record evidence location and control result when copying the evidence is unnecessary.

  • Every recommendation should cite the authority, identify the owner, state the expected proof and explain why it matters to the utility.

  • The standards and legal register should be versioned, reviewed and visibly dated.

Commercial principle

The scan opens the door. The value comes from helping a utility change the way it owns, explains, tests and uses data. The product should support that change, not replace professional judgment with a score.


What the first result page must show

  • The three decisions or data flows that need attention first.

  • The difference between the user's answer and the evidence required to support it.

  • The relevant standards, law or utility obligation in plain language.

  • The accountable seat and the next practical action.

  • A clear invitation to save the result, bring the right people together and begin an evidence-backed consultation.

APPLICATION PAPER

10. The governance backbone for Pump OS, Pipe OS and Reg OS

Three applications should use one governed language for assets, events, rules, evidence, decisions and outcomes.

This publication becomes useful to APAS when it controls how the applications are designed, released and improved. Pump OS, Pipe OS and Reg OS solve different utility problems. They should not create three different definitions of an asset, event, rule, owner, quality result or decision. The common governance spine below is the reusable product foundation.

Product rule

Build a governed record once, connect it through stable identifiers and reuse it wherever the same physical asset, event, obligation or decision appears. A new application may add context. It should not silently create a competing truth.


Figure 19. One governance spine powers three utility operating systems

What this shows. Pump OS, Pipe OS and Reg OS use different operational views, but they should share governed identity, meaning, quality, lineage, rights, rules, evidence, decisions and outcomes. The shared spine prevents each product from rebuilding a different version of truth.

Source: APAS AI product operating model.

What each application operationalizes

Pump OS

Is the pump available, healthy, efficient and safe to run? What work should happen next?

SCADA status and alarms; historian trends; energy; vibration and condition; CMMS or EAM work; asset specifications; operating rules; hydraulic or process model.

A current pump-state and risk product with asset identity, source tags, time, calibration, quality, rule version, work history, operator action and outcome.

The repeatable operating loop

Figure 20. Operationalize one decision chain, then repeat

What this shows. The operating loop starts with a consequential decision, connects its evidence, puts controls into normal work, releases a governed product, monitors use and outcomes, and turns what is learned into the next improvement cycle.

Source: APAS AI implementation method.

  1. Select one consequential decision. State the user, service outcome, consequence and current pain in plain English.

  2. Map the evidence chain. Connect the physical source, system record, transformation, model, rule, person, action and outcome.

  3. Define the data contract. Name the owner, identifiers, meaning, units, quality rules, approved use, access, freshness, retention and change process.

  4. Put controls into normal work. Automate checks where practical and keep a clear human decision where judgment or public accountability is required.

  5. Release the governed product. Show source, time, quality, limits and lineage to the user instead of hiding them in technical logs.

  6. Measure adoption and outcome. Confirm that people use the product and that service, safety, compliance, affordability or delivery improves.

  7. Retest the decision chain. Sample real cases, verify closure, record residual risk and decide what must change.

  8. Reuse the pattern. Carry the same records, controls and evidence methods into the next Pump OS, Pipe OS or Reg OS use case.

Release gates for a usable APAS application

Gate

Question before release

Evidence required

Purpose

Can a utility user explain the decision this feature improves and the harm it helps prevent?

Named user, decision statement, outcome, consequence and product owner.

Data

Can the team explain every important input in simple English and connect it to an approved source?

Data contract, identifier map, source register, quality rules, rights and lineage.

Control

Does the feature detect bad, missing, late, changed or unauthorized data before it misleads a user?

Control design, owner, test results, exceptions, alerts and recovery procedure.

Decision

Is the recommendation separate from the person or rule that has authority to act?

Decision rights, human review, approval record, override reason and escalation path.

Evidence

Could the utility reconstruct the answer during an incident, audit or regulatory challenge?

Retained source, transformation, model or rule version, user action and integrity record.

Outcome

Does the team know whether the feature is used and whether it improves the utility result?

Adoption measure, outcome measure, baseline, target, review cycle and product decision.


Definition of done

  • A utility user can understand the feature, its data and its limits without a data-science translator.

  • The same asset, event, rule and decision identifiers work across the three products where the records overlap.

  • Every important answer displays its source, time, quality state and approved purpose.

  • The responsible, accountable, consulted and informed (RACI) roles are named for product ownership, data ownership, control operation, approval and support.

  • A failed control creates an owned action, a due date, closure proof and a retest.

  • A release has adoption and utility-outcome measures, not only technical completion measures.

  • Support, incident response, data correction, model rollback, supplier exit and record retention are tested before scale.

The usefulness test

If a page, score, model or feature does not help a named utility person make, explain, control or improve a real decision, it is not finished. Operational usefulness is the release standard.

Connector test, permission record, source reconciliation and recovery result.

Decision pattern

Question, rule, evidence, recommendation, human authority, action and outcome.

Decision trace, approval, override record and outcome review.

APPLICATION PAPER

11. A practical 90-day start

Begin with consequential decisions, visible ownership and proof that can be reviewed.

Days 1 to 30 | Frame and select

  • Appoint an executive sponsor and a working owner with authority across operations, data, security, legal and AI.

  • Select three to five material decisions: one operational, one regulatory, one customer, one capital and one AI or analytics use case where applicable.

  • Create the first system, data, interface and owner map for those decisions.

  • Inventory current AI use cases and suppliers. Do not limit the inventory to centrally approved tools.

  • Record immediate legal, regulatory, contract and records obligations for the selected scope.



Days 31 to 60 | Trace and test

  • Trace each selected decision from source to outcome and identify manual steps, spreadsheets, estimates and unowned changes.

  • Test identity, meaning, quality, lineage, access, retention and approval evidence at each handoff.

  • Name an owner and steward for each critical data product or domain in scope.

  • Define the quality requirements by use and consequence, then run the first recurring measures.

  • Review supplier data rights, training-use restrictions, locations, assurance and exit terms.

Days 61 to 90 | Decide and fund

  • Score the selected scope using maturity and evidence confidence. Challenge unsupported ratings.

  • Separate immediate control fixes from operating-model changes and platform work.

  • Approve a 12-month roadmap with owners, dependencies, funding, decision dates and closure evidence.

  • Publish a small executive dashboard: critical decisions covered, evidence gaps, open high-consequence findings, issue age and control results.

  • Schedule the next evidence review and select the next set of decisions to bring into the pattern.

Questions for the executive team

  1. Which utility decisions would cause the most harm if the underlying data were wrong, late or used outside its purpose?

  2. Can we trace those decisions to authoritative sources and reconstruct what happened?

  3. Which person owns the fitness of each critical dataset, not only the system that stores it?

  4. Where are manual transformations and local spreadsheets part of the official decision chain?

  5. Which AI uses could affect service, safety, customers, employees, capital or regulatory outcomes?

  6. What evidence would we need if a regulator, auditor, customer or incident team challenged the decision tomorrow?

  7. Which actions will change the operating system of the utility, and which actions merely close a task?

The 90-day deliverables

Deliverable

Management use

Decision and data map

Shows critical sources, handoffs, owners, suppliers and evidence gaps.

AI and analytics inventory

Shows use, consequence, owner, data source, human role and review state.

Evidence-backed scorecard

Separates maturity from evidence confidence and makes disagreement visible.

Immediate control plan

Names high-consequence fixes, owners, dates and closure proof.

Twelve-month roadmap

Sequences operating model, data products, controls, platforms, adoption and assurance.

Executive risk decision

Records what is funded, accepted, stopped, transferred or scheduled for more work.

APPLICATION PAPER

Closing | The work is to make data usable and accountable

Transformation begins when a utility can explain the decision before it has to defend the incident.

The opportunity in front of utilities is real. AI can help people see patterns, reach information and act with greater speed. The opportunity will not be realized by placing AI on top of data that the organization cannot explain.

Data governance is how a utility turns responsibility into a repeatable system. It gives the operator context, the engineer traceability, the customer a fair process, the executive a clear risk decision, the regulator evidence and the AI system a controlled foundation.

This is not a one-time project. Standards will change. Laws will change. Systems, suppliers, people and risks will change. The living document, the assessment and the application must change with them. The constant is the discipline: write the decision, act through the control, keep the proof and close the gap.

The commitment

We will keep trying to build transformational solutions because the public work deserves more than disconnected transactions. Data-ready before AI-ready. Evidence before assurance. Accountability before scale.

APPLICATION PAPER

Appendix A | The 60 assessment criteria

Each criterion is written as an operating statement and paired with the evidence needed to test it.

The criteria form the working core of the assessment. Not-applicable decisions require a documented scope reason. Source IDs map to Appendix B. The full assessment also records maturity, evidence confidence, consequence, urgency, owner, finding and action.

APPLICATION PAPER

Appendix C | Plain-language glossary

Use the terms consistently in policy, product design, interviews, findings and roadmaps.

Acronym rule

Write the full term first, followed by the short form in parentheses. Use the short form only after that point. Product screens, training, findings and executive reports should follow the same rule.


Term

Working definition

Accountable owner

The person with authority to accept the purpose, fitness, access, lifecycle and risk of a data domain or product.

Advanced metering infrastructure (AMI)

Smart meters, communications and supporting systems that collect and exchange detailed meter information.

Algorithmic impact assessment (AIA)

A structured review of how an automated or AI-supported decision could affect people, services, rights, safety or trust.

American Water Works Association (AWWA)

A water-sector association that publishes standards, manuals, research and professional guidance.

Application programming interface (API)

A controlled way for one software system to request data or a service from another system.

Artificial intelligence (AI)

Software that performs tasks such as prediction, classification, generation or recommendation using learned or encoded methods.

Asset management

The coordinated work used to obtain value from physical assets while managing cost, performance and risk through their life.

Authoritative source

The approved source for a stated use. It may differ by decision and time.

Cloud Data Management Capabilities (CDMC)

An industry framework for governing and controlling data in cloud environments.

Common Information Model (CIM)

A shared model used mainly in the electric-power sector so systems describe network objects and relationships consistently.

Computerized maintenance management system (CMMS)

Software used to plan, assign, record and analyze maintenance, inspections, labor, parts and work orders.

Control

An action or condition designed to prevent, detect or correct an unwanted result.

Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies (COBIT)

A framework for governing and managing enterprise information and technology.

Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP)

Requirements and practices used to protect systems that support essential infrastructure. In North American electricity, CIP also refers to the NERC reliability standards.

Critical data element

A field or record whose failure could materially affect service, safety, compliance, finance, customers or trust.

Customer information system (CIS)

The system that manages customer accounts, service, billing, payments, contacts and related customer records.

Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)

The NIST framework for organizing cybersecurity outcomes across governance, identification, protection, detection, response and recovery.

Data catalog

A searchable inventory that helps people find data and understand its owner, meaning, location, quality, access and use.

Data chaos

A state in which data is fragmented, duplicated, inconsistently defined, unowned or difficult to trace and use with confidence.

Data Catalog Vocabulary (DCAT)

A W3C vocabulary for describing catalogs, datasets, data services and distributions in a consistent way.

Data contract

The agreed purpose, schema, quality, access, lineage, service and lifecycle terms for a data product or interface.

Data Management Association International (DAMA)

A professional association that maintains widely used data-management knowledge and practice guidance.

Data Management Body of Knowledge (DMBOK)

DAMA's reference guide for data governance, architecture, quality, metadata, security and related management practices.

Data Management Capability Assessment Model (DCAM)

An industry model for assessing and improving data-management capability.

Data governance

The decisions, responsibilities, controls and proof used to direct data work.

Data lineage

The route data follows from source through transformation to use.

Data product

A governed dataset, API or feature set with an owner, known users, quality expectations and a service promise.

Data provenance

The history of the data, the activity that affected it and the responsible person or service.

Data quality

Fitness for a stated use, time and consequence.

Data wisdom

The accountable use of governed evidence, operational context, human judgment, consequences and outcome learning.

Data steward

The person who maintains meaning, metadata, rules, issues and consumer communication within an assigned scope.

Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)

A formal review of privacy risks and safeguards for processing that may create high risk to people.

Decision Twin™

An APAS governed decision model connecting operational state, analytical models, rules, evidence, human authority, alternatives, action and outcome learning.

Decision intelligence

The structured use of data, models, rules, alternatives, consequences and evidence to improve a decision while keeping authority explicit.

Digital twin

A digital representation of a physical system that supports state awareness, behavior analysis, scenarios or simulation within a defined scope.

Data Quality Vocabulary (DQV)

A W3C vocabulary for describing data-quality measures, results, annotations and certificates.

Enterprise asset management (EAM)

The people, processes and software used to manage asset information, work, condition, cost and lifecycle decisions across an organization.

Enterprise resource planning (ERP)

Integrated business software for functions such as finance, procurement, inventory, projects and human resources.

Evidence

A retained record that supports a fact, control result, score, decision, action or outcome.

Evidence confidence

The strength of support for a score, from absent or asserted to independently verified.

Exabyte

A unit of digital information equal to 1,000 petabytes or one-thousandth of a zettabyte.

Findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable (FAIR)

Principles that make data easier for people and machines to locate, obtain, combine and use again.

Findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable, open and ethical (FAIROE)

An Anglian Water extension of FAIR that adds openness and ethical use.

Fats, oils and grease (FOG)

Food-related materials that can enter sewers, create blockages and increase overflow risk.

General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)

The European Union law governing personal data, rights, accountability, security and lawful use.

Geographic information system (GIS)

Software and data used to map assets, customers, land, events and other information connected to location.

Historian

A system that stores time-series operating data such as sensor values, alarms, status and calculated measurements.

Industrial automation and control system (IACS)

The hardware and software used to monitor and control industrial processes, equipment and facilities.

International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC)

The international standards organization focused on electrical, electronic and related technologies.

Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)

The standards community that develops many of the technical rules used by the internet.

Integrity

Confidence that data and its evidence remain complete and protected from improper change.

Interoperability

The ability of systems and organizations to exchange data with shared identity, meaning and usable context.

International Organization for Standardization (ISO)

The international body that publishes standards for governance, quality, security, records, assets and many other management areas.

Internet of Things (IoT)

Connected devices and sensors that collect, exchange or act on information about physical conditions.

JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)

A common text format for exchanging structured data between systems.

JavaScript Object Notation for Linked Data (JSON-LD)

A JSON-based format that adds shared identifiers and meaning so connected data can be interpreted consistently.

Key performance indicator (KPI)

A measure used to show whether a service, process, control or product is producing its intended result.

Laboratory information management system (LIMS)

Software that manages samples, methods, instruments, custody, results, approval, amendments and laboratory records.

Machine learning (ML)

A form of AI in which a model learns patterns from data to classify, predict or generate an output.

Metadata

Information that identifies, describes, locates, classifies and explains data.

National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

A United States agency that publishes widely used risk, cybersecurity, privacy, AI, control and measurement guidance.

North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC)

The organization responsible for reliability standards for the North American bulk electric system.

Network and Information Systems Directive 2 (NIS2)

A European Union cybersecurity directive that adds management and risk duties for important and essential sectors.

Observability

The ability to see the health, freshness, quality and failure state of data and pipelines.

Open Digital Rights Language (ODRL)

A W3C language for expressing permissions, prohibitions, duties and conditions for data or digital resources.

Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC)

An international organization that develops standards for location, mapping, sensors and geospatial information.

Open, shared or closed

A deliberate classification that balances access and value against privacy, security, commercial, quality and misuse risk.

Petabyte

A unit of digital information equal to 1,000 terabytes.

OpenLineage

An open specification for recording how jobs, runs and datasets are connected in data processing.

Open Security Controls Assessment Language (OSCAL)

A NIST format for expressing security controls, implementation details, assessment plans and results in machine-readable form.

Office of Management and Budget (OMB)

The United States federal office that issues management and budget policy, including federal data and AI memoranda.

Operating system (OS)

In this publication, an APAS product layer that joins governed data, rules, workflow, evidence and outcomes for a utility decision area. It does not mean a computer operating system.

Operational technology (OT)

Hardware and software that monitor or control physical utility processes and equipment.

Operational Twin

A connected view of current physical state together with asset, work, environmental and operator context.

Personally identifiable information (PII)

Information that identifies a person directly or can identify the person when combined with other information.

Privacy impact assessment (PIA)

A structured review of how a project or system collects, uses, shares, protects and retains personal data.

Professional Engineer (P.E.)

A licensed engineering credential in the United States. Requirements and authority depend on the jurisdiction.

Provenance Data Model (PROV)

The W3C model that represents data or other entities, the activities that affected them and the people or systems responsible.

Public Utilities Board (PUB)

Singapore's national water agency. PUB is the agency's current public name and originated from Public Utilities Board.

Pump Operating System (Pump OS)

The APAS application concept that connects pump state, condition, work, energy, operating rules, decisions and outcomes.

Pipe Operating System (Pipe OS)

The APAS application concept that connects pipe identity, condition, flow, failure, customer consequence, work, renewal and outcomes.

Regulatory Operating System (Reg OS)

The APAS application concept that connects obligations, limits, authoritative data, calculations, approvals, filings, evidence and corrective action.

Responsible, accountable, consulted and informed (RACI)

A role pattern used to clarify who does the work, who owns the result, who provides input and who must be kept informed.

Resource Description Framework (RDF)

A W3C model for representing data as identified things and relationships that machines can connect and interpret.

Residual risk

Risk that remains after controls and is accepted, transferred, avoided or scheduled for more action.

Risk Management Framework (RMF)

A structured method for identifying risk, selecting controls, assessing results, authorizing use and monitoring change.

Recovery point objective (RPO)

The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time after a disruption.

Recovery time objective (RTO)

The target time for restoring a system, service or data product after a disruption.

Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL)

A W3C language for testing whether graph data follows required structures and rules.

Simple Knowledge Organization System (SKOS)

A W3C model for controlled vocabularies such as taxonomies, thesauri and code lists.

Sensor, Observation, Sample and Actuator (SOSA)

A lightweight W3C and OGC model for describing sensors, observations, samples, actuators and related activities.

Semantic Sensor Network ontology (SSN)

A W3C and OGC model that adds detailed system and deployment meaning to sensor and observation data.

Source system

The system or record from which data is obtained. It is not automatically authoritative for every use.

Supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA)

The industrial system used to monitor equipment and processes, collect operating data, issue alarms and support remote control.

Tag

A named SCADA or historian point representing a measurement, status, command, alarm or calculated value.

Terabyte

A unit of digital information equal to 1,000 gigabytes.

Traceability

The ability to follow a requirement, record or decision backward and forward through linked evidence.

Transformation

A change that improves how the utility decides, operates and learns, not only the completion of a task.

World Wide Web Consortium (W3C)

The organization that develops open web standards, including standards for provenance, data catalogs, linked data, constraints and digital rights.

Work order

The controlled record used to request, plan, perform, close and review maintenance, inspection, repair or field work.

Zettabyte

A unit of digital information equal to 1,000 exabytes, 1 million petabytes or 1 billion terabytes.

APPLICATION PAPER

Appendix D | Validation protocol, worked example and release gates

Use the method without allowing a publication score to become an unsupported product, benchmark or assurance claim.

Figure 21. Four release gates prevent one score from making four different claims

What this shows. Publication readiness, assessment-method validation, application security and operational readiness, and independent assurance are separate decisions. Passing one gate does not pass the others.

Source: APAS AI release-governance model.

Four separate release decisions

Gate

Decision

Minimum evidence

Accountable approval

Publication readiness

May the paper be published with its stated scope and limits?

Verified sources, complete references, resolved production defects, accessibility review and change record.

Publication owner and editorial reviewer.

Assessment-method validation

May scores be compared, benchmarked or used without facilitation?

Diverse pilots, scoring calibration, inter-rater reliability, sensitivity tests, utility overlays and worked examples.

Method owner with independent technical challenge.

Application readiness

May the product accept utility evidence or connect to utility systems?

Threat model, privacy assessment, records and residency design, supplier controls, safe integration boundary, incident plan and user testing.

Product, security, privacy, records and utility-operations owners.

Independent assurance

May APAS issue certification, compliance or assurance conclusions?

Defined criteria, competence, independence, sampling, evidence retention, quality controls and external review authority.

Qualified independent assurance authority.


Release rule

A pass at the publication gate does not pass the method, application or assurance gates. No average score can override a failed safety, privacy, legal, evidence or independence condition.


Utility-type overlays

The 60 core criteria remain stable, but the critical data, consequence and required evidence must change by utility context. The overlay does not create a separate governance system. It changes the decision samples, operating risks and evidence depth used to test the common system.

Overlay

Priority decisions

Critical data and evidence

Drinking water

Treatment release, pressure, water quality, source protection and customer notice.

SCADA and historian context; laboratory custody and method; distribution model; asset condition; permit limits; operator authorization.

Wastewater and stormwater

Overflow response, wet-weather operation, collection risk, treatment performance and discharge reporting.

Rainfall; levels and flows; pump state; sewer model; blockage and FOG work; event timeline; consent or permit evidence.

Electric

Switching, outage restoration, load and voltage control, asset health and reliability reporting.

Network model; telemetry; protection settings; outage and work records; asset hierarchy; NERC applicability; operator and control evidence.

Multi-utility

Cross-service customer, emergency, capital, cyber and shared-infrastructure decisions.

Common asset and location identity; service boundaries; shared suppliers; access segregation; coordinated incident and records evidence.


Worked assessment example with missing and conflicting evidence

Example decision: a wet-weather overflow response. The assessment begins with an asserted maturity of Level 4 because a dashboard, procedure and monthly review exist. The evidence sample shows that one SCADA tag lacks a governed unit, rainfall time is offset by one hour, the spreadsheet transformation has no version record, and operator approval is not linked to the regulatory response.

Measure

Initial answer

Evidence result

Recorded outcome

Maturity

4, measured

The process operates, but critical handoffs are not controlled.

2, defined. A score cannot exceed Level 2 until recurring evidence supports operation.

Evidence confidence

3, operating sample

Two sources verified, two partial, one missing and one conflicting.

2, documented. Conflict and missing approval remain visible.

Consequence

5

Potential service, environmental, regulatory and public-trust harm.

5. Consequence is not reduced by a lower maturity score.

Urgency

4

Wet-weather season begins in 45 days.

4. Fund immediate control correction and a retest.

Finding

None

Authoritative time, transformation version and approval evidence are incomplete.

High priority. Owner, action, date and closure proof required.


Missing-evidence rule

Absence is recorded as absence. It is not converted into a neutral answer. Conflicting evidence lowers confidence, triggers adjudication and remains linked to the score until resolved.


Scoring sensitivity test

Sensitivity testing asks whether a reasonable change in weights or evidence confidence changes the roadmap. If a priority disappears only because one weight changed, the recommendation is unstable and must be challenged before funding.

Scenario

Evidence weight

Result

Management interpretation

Act now.

Priority is stable.

Not averaged

A critical failure cannot be hidden by strong scores elsewhere.


Minimum data contract and provenance event

Record

Required fields

Control purpose

Data product contract

Product ID, purpose, owner, consumers, schema, units, source, quality rules, access, rights, lineage, service level, retention and version.

Makes the approved use and service promise explicit.

Provenance event

Event ID, input IDs, output ID, activity, responsible agent, time, code or configuration version, purpose, quality result, approval and integrity evidence.

Reconstructs what happened, when, why and by whom.

Control result

Control ID, design owner, test time, sample, expected result, actual result, exception, reviewer and retained evidence location.

Shows whether the control operated and what failed.

Assessment finding

Finding ID, criterion, sampled decision, evidence state, cause, consequence, owner, action, due date, closure proof and retest result.

Keeps the score connected to accountable improvement.


Calibration and assessor-reliability protocol

  1. Select at least three utilities that differ in size, ownership, service type and regulatory setting.

  2. Choose the same minimum decision samples and record where an overlay changes the evidence requirement.

  3. Have at least two qualified assessors score the same evidence independently before discussion.

  4. Compare criterion agreement, domain agreement, evidence-confidence agreement and finding severity.

  5. Adjudicate disagreements using the retained evidence and scoring rules, then update examples without hiding the original result.

  6. Run weight and missing-evidence sensitivity tests and publish any change to priority or roadmap sequence.

  7. Approve a benchmark only after the sample, method, limitations and uncertainty are visible and repeatable.

Conflict, correction and portability rules

  • Disclose when the assessor may sell implementation work arising from the assessment.

  • Allow the utility to challenge a score and retain the evidence, reasoning, decision and resolution.

  • Keep client evidence portable through exportable records and stable identifiers.

  • Publish material corrections, affected criteria, reason, approver and effective date.

  • Retain prior versions so a result can be reconstructed under the method used at the time.

Living-document control

Trigger

Required update

New or revised standard

Record edition, status, affected criteria, implementation decision and next review.

New law, rule or regulator action

Confirm applicability, effective date, owner, evidence and legal review.

Quarterly review

Recertify priority sources, links, open findings, scores, ownership and roadmap status.
